items.description: The input mode for audio or video.

items.description: Audio sample rate (0-96000, max allowed by PCM16L).

items.description: Audio channel count (1-2, max allowed by PCM16L). With 2 channels the audio is encoded in stereo.

items.description: The input media source.

items.name: keep_open: bool
items.description: If set to true, the stream will be kept open and changes are detected automatically when the input differs from the previous one, otherwise if set to false, the stream change is always forced.

items.name: bitrate: Optional[int]
items.description: Opus encoder bitrate in bits per second (6000-510000). If not set, the WebRTC default is used, 32 kbps in mono and 64 kbps in stereo.

items.name: format: Optional[ntgcalls.Format]
items.description: Format of the audio exchanged with the source or the destination, Ogg (Opus) if not set. Ignored for devices. Sending Ogg Opus skips the audio encoding and keeps the original quality, since the packets are sent without being encoded again, and are re-encoded only when they don't match the requested channels or bitrate. When recording to a file or a shell command in Ogg, a single participant is written as-is, while more participants are decoded, mixed and re-encoded, which uses more CPU than recording in PCM.

items.name: max_delay_ms: Optional[int]
items.description: Longest time in milliseconds to wait for a late Opus packet when receiving Ogg Opus, 1000 if not set. Received packets go through a jitter buffer that adapts to the connection up to this limit, and a packet that doesn't arrive in time is rebuilt from the next one. A lower value lowers the latency of live frames, while a higher value loses fewer packets on unstable connections. Ignored for PCM.

items.description: Format of the video read from the source, Matroska if not set. Ignored for devices and desktop capture. A Matroska stream carrying H264 without B-frames, VP8, VP9 or AV1 is sent without re-encoding when it matches the negotiated codec, and re-encoded only when it doesn't, or briefly when a viewer needs a keyframe. When playing back to a file or a shell command, I420 composes every participant into an animated grid at the given size and frame rate, while Matroska writes a single participant as received and decodes, composes and re-encodes when there are more, which uses more CPU. entries.title: Introduction
entries.description:
Being a modern library, NTgCalls requires CMake 3.27+ and Python 3.10+ to be built on your system. On Linux it also needs libasound2 and libpulse-dev. We recommend using the latest version of CMake.
IMPORTANT
Before building NTgCalls, check for pre-compiled shared libs on GitHub Releases, Python bindings on PyPI, the Node.js package on npm or the crate on crates.io. Building from source may be necessary if pre-compiled packages are not available.
NOTE
On Linux x86_64, macOS and Android the build downloads its own Clang toolchain, so there is nothing to install by hand. Linux ARM64 is the only platform that uses the system compiler.

Installing Prerequisites

Below, we will guide you through the step-by-step process of installing the prerequisites required to compile NTgCalls on your operating system.

Linux

  1. Update the system's package list:
    First, make sure you have an updated list of packages: 
    $ sudo apt update
  2. Install the build dependencies:
    On ARM64 the toolchain is not downloaded, so Clang has to come from the system:

Windows

  1. Install Microsoft Visual Studio 2022:
    Install Microsoft Visual Studio 2022 with the C++ workload. You can download it from the official website.
  2. Download CMake Installer:
    Download the CMake installer for Windows from the official website.
  3. Run Installer:
    Run the downloaded CMake installer and follow the installation wizard instructions. Make sure to select the option to add CMake to the system PATH during installation.

macOS

  1. Install Xcode Command Line Tools:
    If you don't have Xcode installed, you can install the Command Line Tools separately. Open a terminal and run the following command: 
    $ xcode-select --install
  2. Install CMake:
    Open a terminal and run the following command to install CMake: 
    $ brew install cmake

Cloning and Building

In this section, you'll learn how to clone the NTgCalls repository and build the library from source.

Cloning the Repo

To begin building NTgCalls from source, you need to clone the GitHub repository. Follow these steps to clone the repo:
  1. Change to the Directory Where You Want to Clone the Repo:
    Navigate to the directory where you want to store the NTgCalls source code. You can use the cd command to change directories. 
    $ cd /path/to/your/directory
  2. Clone the NTgCalls Repository:
    Use the following command to clone the NTgCalls GitHub repository: 
    $ git clone https://github.com/pytgcalls/ntgcalls.git --recursive

Compilation

Every binding is built through the same entry point, setup.py build_lib, which takes the target you want and reads how to build it from that target's own configuration. Run every command from the root directory of the project.
IMPORTANT
It's essential to have Python 3.10+ installed on your system.

Shared Library

For developers looking to use NTgCalls with C and C++, we provide C bindings. This is the default target, so it needs no --target: The libraries and the generated ntgcalls.h are written to shared-output or static-output.

Python Bindings

The Python bindings are installed like any other package, and the extension is compiled as part of the install: 
$ pip3 install . -U

Node.js Bindings

The Node.js addon is built through the same command, and lands in targets/node/build/Release: 
$ python3 setup.py build_lib --target=node

Rust Crate

The crate links against the C shared library. Build it once, then point the crate at the result through NTGCALLS_LIB_DIR, otherwise the build script downloads the matching release from GitHub: 
$ python3 setup.py build_lib --static
$ NTGCALLS_LIB_DIR=$PWD/static-output/lib cargo build --manifest-path targets/rust/Cargo.toml

Java for Android Bindings

The Android target builds the native libraries for all four ABIs, then Gradle packs them into the archive:
  1. Generate the .so libraries for the Android platform: 
    $ python3 setup.py build_lib --target=android
  2. Build the Android project: 
    $ cd targets/android
$ ./gradlew build assembleRelease
  3. Get the .aar file:
    Copy the generated .aar file to your desired directory: 
    $ cp app/build/outputs/aar/app-release.aar /path/to/your/directory

Other Options

build_lib also accepts --no-preserve-cache to drop the build directory once it is done, and --defines=key=value;key2=value2 to override any substitution the target configuration uses. Two more commands are available: list_targets prints the targets that can be built, and generate writes the language-agnostic schema every binding and the documentation are generated from, without building anything. 
$ python3 setup.py list_targets
$ python3 setup.py generate

entries.title: Client
entries.description:
The NTgCalls Client is your primary interface for interacting with Telegram Calls. This page covers what surrounds the API: how to create and dispose of an instance, how to read the library version, and how to route the library logs into your own logging setup. Everything else is documented in the Reference section.

Logging

The library reports its own diagnostics and the ones coming from WebRTC. How they reach you depends on the binding.

Callbacks

Every callback is registered on the instance and documented, one page each, in the Callbacks section of the Reference.
NOTE
When registering callbacks, keep in mind that each registration replaces the previously set callback.

Welcome to this section, which is primarily intended for developers who are moderately experienced or seeking to perform a porting in their language using C bindings. If you are new to Python development, we strongly recommend using Py-TgCalls. However, if you fall into the aforementioned categories, you can find an example of usage with the various porting below.

Recommended Projects by the Community

Community and Official Libraries

In the following section, we present a comprehensive catalog of libraries, thoughtfully crafted by the community and officially endorsed, all of which leverage the robust capabilities of NTgCalls.

entries.title: Idle
entries.description: This function will run indefinitely in order to block the main script execution and prevent it from exiting while having client(s) that are still running in the background. Py-TgCalls works by keeping your handlers in a pool of worker threads, which run concurrently outside the main thread. Calling idle() will ensure that the client(s) remain active, by preventing the main script from ending until you decide to quit. Once a signal is received (e.g.: from CTRL+C) the function will terminate and your main script will continue.

entries.title: Calling Methods
entries.description:
At this point, we have successfully installed Py-TgCalls and installed an MTProto client; we are now aiming towards the core of the library. It’s time to start playing with the API!

Basic Usage

Making API method calls with Py-TgCalls is very simple. Here’s a basic example we are going to examine step by step:
from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls
from pytgcalls import idle
...
api_id = 12345
api_hash = '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef'
...
app = PyTgCalls(client)
app.start()
app.play(
    -1001185324811,
    'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4',
)
idle()

Basic step-by-step

  1. Let’s begin by importing the Client class and idle function: 
    from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls
from pytgcalls import idle
  2. Now let’s import your MTProto Client:
  3. Set your api_id and api_hash taken from my.telegram.org: 
    api_id = 12345
api_hash = '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef'
  4. Initialize the MTProto client:
  5. Initialize the Py-TgCalls client: 
    app = PyTgCalls(client)
  6. Start the Py-TgCalls client: 
    app.start()
  7. Now you can call any method you want: 
    app.play(
    -1001185324811,
    'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4',
)
  8. Lastly, call the idle function to keep your code running: 
    idle()

Asynchronous Calls

In case you wish to run Py-TgCalls asynchronously:
import asyncio
from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls
from pytgcalls import idle
...
app = PyTgCalls(client)

async def main():
    await app.start()
    await app.play(
        -1001185324811,
        'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4',
    )
    await idle()

asyncio.run(main())

Asynchronous step-by-step

  1. Import Py-TgCalls, AsyncIO and create an instance: 
    import asyncio
from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls
from pytgcalls import idle
...
app = PyTgCalls(client)
  2. Async methods can’t be executed at the top level, because they must be within an async-defined function; here, we define one, and we put our code inside it; method calls require the await keyword: 
    async def main():
    await app.start()
    await app.play(
        -1001185324811,
        'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4',
    )
    await idle()
  3. Then, we tell asyncio to call main() in async mode 
    asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(main())

entries.description:
Private Calls, Code Rework, Async Support and more!

What's new?

  • Private Calls: Now you can make private calls by just using a single method for also group calls, by using play().
  • Code Rework: The code has been reworked to improve performance, stability and to make it more readable.
  • Async Support: NTgCalls now supports asynchronous methods for improved performance.
  • Filters for Updates: Added filters for updates to allow for more granular control over updates, More Info.
  • Improved Documentation: Updated documentation with more examples, new UI and comprehensive guidance.
  • Bug Fixes: Addressed various bugs for a more stable experience.

Breaking Changes

  • Now methods like change_stream() and join_group_call() was removed, now you can use play() for both private, group calls and changing streams. 
      # Change stream
- call_py.change_stream(
+ call_py.play(
      -1001234567890,
      AudioPiped(
          'input.mp4',
      ),
  )
  
  # Join group call
- call_py.join_group_call(
+ call_py.play(
      -1001234567890,
      AudioPiped(
          'input.mp4',
      ),
  )

  • Now all listeners like on_stream_end() was unified in on_update() and with filters, for example: 
    + from pytgcalls import filters
+ from pytgcalls.types import ChatUpdate
  ...
  # On Closed Voice Chat
- @call_py.on_closed_voice_chat()
+ @call_py.on_update(filters.chat_update(ChatUpdate.Status.CLOSED_VOICE_CHAT))
  async def on_closed_voice_chat(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update):
      print(update)
  
  # On stream end
- @call_py.on_stream_end()
+ @call_py.on_update(filters.stream_end)
  async def on_stream_end(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update):
      print(update)

  • Reworked GroupCall type, now is Call and now is more powerful and easy to use.
  • Removed JoinedGroupCallParticipant and LeftGroupCallParticipant classes, now you can see the action in GroupCallParticipant class.
  • Removed all legacy types and input stream, now is a mandatory to use MediaStream for all streams.
  • Now ping() from Client is not anymore a coroutine, now is a normal method.
  • Removed get_active_call() and get_call(), now is a mandatory to use calls() from Client.
  • Renamed leave_group_call to leave_call().
  • Moved MediaStream flags under MediaStream.Flags instead of MediaStream.
  • Now invite_hash, join_as and auto_start are part of GroupCallConfig instead of join_group_call.
  • Renamed additional_ffmpeg_parameters to ffmpeg_parameters in MediaStream.
  • For more info about breaking changes, check the Examples, if we missed something, please open an issue.

Additional Notes

We're pleased to announce that now is available an unofficial porting of NTgCalls for Rust, for more info, check the repository.

entries.description:
Support for Large Group Calls, RTMP Streams, and More!

What's new?

  • Support for Large Group Calls: Py-TgCalls now supports group calls with 20 or more participants in channels, allowing the deprecation of the UnMuteNeeded exception.
  • RTMP Stream Integration: You can now connect to RTMP streams and record them using the record() method. This enables streaming external RTMP content directly into your group calls.
  • Group Call Discarding Option: The close parameter has been added to the leave_call() method, allowing you to fully terminate a group call when it's no longer needed.

entries.title: Changelog 4.0.X: Py-TgCalls v4.0.X
entries.description:
Studio-Quality Audio, Lower CPU and Video Recording!

What's new?

  • Opus Passthrough: When the audio is already Opus, as in WebM, Ogg and most YouTube streams, it is sent without decoding and re-encoding, keeping its original quality and skipping the CPU spent on audio encoding.
  • Video Passthrough: H264 without B-frames, VP8, VP9 and AV1 videos are sent as they are, saving most of the CPU spent on video. A viewer joining the call still gets a picture right away, and the video is re-encoded automatically when it doesn't match the call or the bandwidth drops.
  • Video Recording: RecordStream now records the camera and the screen sharing to a file, composing the participants into an animated grid.
  • Stutter-Free Opus Recording: Received Opus goes through a jitter buffer that adapts to the connection, and late or lost packets are rebuilt instead of becoming silence, so recordings and external frames stay smooth even when the call comes from a distant data center. The new max_delay_ms parameter of AudioDescription caps how long it waits for a late packet.
  • Lightweight Recording: .opus and .mkv recordings are written without FFmpeg, saving a single participant exactly as received.
  • Compressed External Media: The new Format selects compressed or raw media, and FrameData now carries the Codec and keyframe flag of each frame, so Opus packets and compressed video can be sent and received directly.
  • Studio-Grade Audio: Audio now reaches listeners up to 90% closer to the original in our tests, with richer highs and full stereo separation.
  • Audio Quality Control: The new bitrate parameter of AudioParameters and AudioDescription lets you pick the audio quality, and it can be changed while the call is running.
  • New Audio Presets: AudioQuality STUDIO and HIGH now stream in stereo at a much higher quality, the new MASTER preset streams at the maximum Opus bitrate of 510 kbps, and the new VOICE preset sounds like the official Telegram clients.
  • Group Call Messages: Read, send and delete the messages of the group call chat with send_message(), delete_messages() and the new filters.call_message() filter, with formatting through Telegram Bot API HTML.
  • musl Support: NTgCalls now ships musllinux builds for x86_64 and arm64 on PyPI, npm and crates.io, so it runs on Alpine Linux out of the box.
  • Automatic Rejoin: Like the official clients, Py-TgCalls now checks whether it is still in the call while reconnecting and rejoins on its own when Telegram drops it, when the end-to-end encryption of a conference fails or when the stream reports that the userbot left. The stream keeps playing from where it was, and the screen sharing and the invite link are restored.
  • Conference Participant Tracking: Participants who left an end-to-end encrypted conference are removed from its blockchain, so they can no longer decrypt it, and GroupCallParticipant now reports through has_e2e_key whether each participant holds the key.
  • Clearer Errors: A missing FFmpeg now raises a clear No executable found for the command error instead of an internal one.
  • Optional Arguments: Optional fields of NTgCalls types can now be omitted in Python and Java, so MediaDescription(microphone=...) works without passing every source.
  • Bug Fixes: Addressed various bugs for a more stable experience.

Breaking Changes

  • The bitrate parameter of AudioParameters has been renamed to sample_rate, while bitrate now sets the Opus encoder bitrate. 
      from pytgcalls.types.raw import AudioParameters
  
  AudioParameters(
-     bitrate=48000,
+     sample_rate=48000,
      channels=2,
+     bitrate=128000,
  )

  • The default AudioQuality.HIGH now streams in stereo at a higher quality, which uses more upload bandwidth. Use AudioQuality.VOICE to keep the previous outgoing audio.
  • NTgCalls now expects compressed media by default: AudioDescription reads Ogg Opus and VideoDescription reads Matroska. Raw PCM and I420 sources now need the format parameter. The Py-TgCalls raw AudioStream and VideoStream keep PCM and I420 as their default. 
    - from ntgcalls import AudioDescription, MediaSource
+ from ntgcalls import AudioDescription, Format, MediaSource
  
  AudioDescription(
      MediaSource.SHELL, 48000, 2,
      'ffmpeg -i input.mp3 -f s16le pipe:1', False,
+     format=Format.PCM,
  )

  • FrameData now requires the codec and keyframe of the frame. send_frame() fills them in for raw frames when they are not given. 
    - from ntgcalls import FrameData, VideoRotation
+ from ntgcalls import Codec, FrameData, VideoRotation
  
- FrameData(0, VideoRotation.VIDEO_ROTATION_0, 1280, 720)
+ FrameData(0, VideoRotation.VIDEO_ROTATION_0, 1280, 720, Codec.I420, True)

entries.title: Handling Updates
entries.description:
Calling API methods sequentially is cool, but what if, for example, the list of participants changes? This page covers updates and how to handle such events in PyTgCalls. Let’s have a look at how they work.

Defining Updates

First of all, let's define what these updates are. As hinted earlier, updates are events that happen in Py-TgCalls, such as joining a group call, changes in the participant list, stream ended etc. They are meant to notify you about a new specific state change. These updates are handled by registering one or more callback functions in your app using Decorators. Each handler deals with a specific event. When a matching update arrives from Telegram or NTgCalls, the registered callback function will be called back by the framework, and its body will execute.

Registering a Handler

To explain how handlers work, let's examine the one that will be in charge of handling StreamEnded updates for video streams, which occur when a video stream ends. The same setup logic is shared with every type of handler, and you should not have trouble setting them up once you have learned from this section.
NOTE
You can mix def and async def handlers as much as you need, Py-TgCalls will still work concurrently and efficiently regardless of what you choose.

Using Decorators

The most elegant way to register a stream end handler is by using the on_update() decorator together with the stream_end() filter:
from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls, filters
from pytgcalls.types import StreamEnded
from pytgcalls.types import Update
...
app = PyTgCalls(client)

@app.on_update(filters.stream_end(StreamEnded.Type.VIDEO))
async def my_handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update):
    await client.play(
        update.chat_id,
        'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4',
    )

app.run()
The defined my_handler function, which accepts two arguments (client, update), will be executed whenever a new update arrives.

Using add_handler()

The add_handler() method takes any handler instance that wraps around your defined callback function and registers it in your Client. It is useful in case you want to programmatically add handlers.
from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls, filters
from pytgcalls.types import StreamEnded
from pytgcalls.types import Update
...
app = PyTgCalls(client)

async def my_handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update):
    await client.play(
        update.chat_id,
        'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4',
    )

app.add_handler(my_handler, filters.stream_end(StreamEnded.Type.VIDEO))
app.run()

entries.title: Install Guide
entries.description:
Being a modern Python library, Py-TgCalls requires Python 3.10+ to be installed in your system. We recommend using the latest versions of both Python 3 and pip.
  • Get Python 3 from the Python website or use your package manager.
  • Get pip by following the instructions here.
IMPORTANT
Py-TgCalls only supports Python 3, starting from version 3.10.

Install Py-TgCalls

The easiest way to install and upgrade Py-TgCalls to its latest stable version is by using pip:
$ pip3 install -U py-tgcalls

Bleeding Edge

Py-TgCalls is always evolving: although new releases on PyPI are only published when a significant number of changes are added, this doesn’t mean you can’t try new features right now! In case you’d like to try out the latest Py-TgCalls’ features, the GitHub repo is constantly updated with new changes; you can install the development version straight from the master branch using this command (note “master.zip” in the link):
$ pip3 install -U git+https://github.com/pytgcalls/pytgcalls

Verifying

To verify that Py-TgCalls is correctly installed, open a Python shell and import it. If no errors show up you are good to go.
>>> import pytgcalls
>>> pytgcalls.__version__
'4.0.0b4'

entries.title: Quick Start
entries.description:
The next few steps serve as a quick start for all new Pythoneers that want to see Py-TgCalls in action as quickly as possible. Let’s go!

Get Py-TgCalls Real Fast

  1. Install Py-TgCalls with pip3 install -U py-tgcalls.
  2. Choose your MTProto client between PyrogramMod (ex Pyrogram) and Telethon.
  3. Get your own Telegram API key from my.telegram.org
  4. Open your favorite text editor and use the following: 
    from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls
from pytgcalls import idle
...
chat_id = -1001185324811
app = PyTgCalls(client)
app.start()
app.play(
    chat_id,
    'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4',
)
idle()
  5. Replace client and chat_id values with your own.
  6. Save the file as main.py.
  7. Watch Py-TgCalls playing the audio file.
  8. Join our community.

Enjoy the API

That was just a brief overview that barely scratched the surface! In the following few pages of the introduction, we’ll have a much more in-depth look at what we have just done. Are you feeling eager to continue? You can take a shortcut to Call Methods and return later to learn more details.

entries.title: Using Handlers
entries.description:
Handlers are used to instruct Py-TgCalls to execute a specific function when a certain event occurs. For a much more convenient way to handle updates, you can use the decorators instead.

Registering Handlers

To register a handler, you need to use the add_handler method. This method takes two arguments: the first is the callback function, and the second is the filter.
from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls
from pytgcalls.types import Update
from pytgcalls import filters as call_filters
...

client = # Here Your MTProto Client
app = PyTgCalls(client)

async def handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update):
    print(update)
...
app.add_handler(handler, call_filters.stream_end())
...

Removing Handlers

To remove a handler, you need to use the remove_handler method. This method takes the callback function as its only argument.
from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls
from pytgcalls.types import Update
...

client = # Here Your MTProto Client
app = PyTgCalls(client)

async def handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update):
    print(update)
...
app.remove_handler(handler)
...
